name: Ant Design
fit: Feature-rich business applications, administration, complex forms and CRUD workflows.
pros: Broad component catalog; consistent form and table patterns; tokens and an extensive companion ecosystem.
cons: A recognizable visual language; advanced patterns can introduce several companion packages and more configuration.
note: Distinguish antd from ProComponents, the Ant Design Pro starter, Ant Design Charts and Ant Design X. “Pro” does not by itself mean a paid edition.

name: Atlassian Design System
fit: Products integrated with Atlassian and collaboration interfaces with similar interaction needs.
pros: Detailed foundations, content guidance and collaboration-oriented components.
cons: Design-system licensing is tied to Atlassian integrations; package and asset permissions require careful separation.
note: ADS terms include an open-source carveout. Check each exact package license; neither a blanket prohibition nor blanket permission for all Atlaskit assets is accurate.

name: Base UI
fit: A custom visual identity backed by composable interaction primitives.
pros: Unstyled components; open composition; accessibility-focused behavior; freedom to choose a CSS approach.
cons: You must supply visual design, tokens, layouts and larger application patterns; it is not an enterprise application suite.
note: Compare the actual controls and composition model with Radix and React Aria. Base UI is distinct from Material UI despite shared origins.

name: IBM Carbon
fit: Enterprise platforms that need a disciplined visual language and consistent data presentation.
pros: Extensive design guidance, tokens, UI shell and data-table patterns; a separate Carbon Charts ecosystem.
cons: The IBM visual character is strong; richer product workflows may need companion packages or application composition.
note: Separate core Carbon, Carbon Charts and IBM Products components when checking coverage and compatibility. Not every package has the same lifecycle.

name: Clarity
fit: Angular-based management consoles and structured enterprise administration.
pros: Enterprise interaction guidance; data-oriented Angular components; coordinated visual styles and icons.
cons: The active Angular offering is a different adoption path from the old framework-neutral Core package.
note: Clarity Core’s Web Components repository is archived. Do not treat old React/Vue examples as evidence of an actively maintained equivalent to Clarity Angular.

name: Cloudscape
fit: Resource management, operations consoles and workflows combining collections, detail views and guided tasks.
pros: Integrated layouts, property filters, tables, split panels, wizards and detailed usage patterns.
cons: Opinionated console structure; a distinct visual character; current chart wrappers introduce a separate Highcharts dependency.
note: The UI is not limited to AWS-backed products. Core open-source licensing does not remove the need to check Highcharts terms when using the new charts.

name: Fluent 2
fit: Productivity tools, collaboration apps and experiences seeking a Microsoft-familiar visual language.
pros: Cross-platform design guidance, tokens, themes and well-developed interaction patterns.
cons: Web, native and older Fluent implementations are not interchangeable; verify component and token parity for your platform.
note: Choose the intended Fluent generation and implementation explicitly. Microsoft ecosystem familiarity is a benefit, not a requirement to use Microsoft backend services.

name: FlyonUI
fit: Fast Tailwind-based interfaces where prebuilt styling and markup are useful.
pros: Semantic component classes, themes and a broad set of interface elements and integrations.
cons: JavaScript initialization and framework lifecycles need integration work; complex widgets may depend on third-party plugins.
note: The original code is MIT, but the current license page also describes bundled Preline dual-license terms. Review those terms and any paid templates separately.

name: Material UI
fit: General-purpose web applications that benefit from familiar Material components and a large React ecosystem.
pros: Broad styled component coverage, theming, documentation and optional MUI X grids, pickers and charts.
cons: Material styling may need deliberate adaptation; advanced MUI X features can require commercial licenses.
note: Material UI and MUI X are separate product layers. Compare Community, Pro and Premium against required features; do not infer full grid capability from the free core library.

name: PatternFly
fit: Infrastructure, developer tools and operational administration with dense, task-focused workflows.
pros: Console-oriented patterns, data views, wizards and extensions for specialist operational experiences.
cons: Its operations aesthetic may be less natural for consumer or brand-led products; extensions add their own integration surface.
note: Inventory core components and extensions separately. Red Hat origins do not restrict it to Red Hat products or infrastructure.

name: Primer
fit: Developer-facing tools, repositories, collaboration and structured content workflows.
pros: GitHub-familiar interaction language, tokens, Octicons and product patterns for search, navigation and editing.
cons: A recognizable developer-tool aesthetic; some documented shared components are internal rather than general public APIs.
note: Distinguish Product UI from Brand UI, and check the status and public availability of each component before planning around it.

name: Radix Primitives
fit: Teams building a bespoke design system or adding accessible controls incrementally.
pros: Unstyled, granular primitives; focus and keyboard behavior; flexible composition and styling.
cons: Visual design, higher-level workflows, data grids and charting remain your responsibility.
note: Radix Primitives and Radix Themes are different offerings. A styled documentation example does not mean Primitives ships that appearance.

name: React Aria Components
fit: Custom interfaces where accessibility, internationalization and complex input behavior are central.
pros: Style-free components, adaptive interactions, keyboard behavior and internationalization support.
cons: Requires a visual system and application-level composition; the styling and state APIs need team familiarity.
note: React Aria Components is the unstyled component layer. It is distinct from the lower-level hooks and the styled React Spectrum system.

name: React Spectrum
fit: Accessible, adaptive web applications comfortable with Adobe’s Spectrum visual language.
pros: Coordinated styled components, light/dark modes, adaptive input behavior and internationalization.
cons: The Spectrum identity is a deliberate constraint; bespoke brand expression may be easier with an unstyled foundation.
note: Choose Spectrum for the styled system and React Aria for visual freedom. They share an ecosystem but solve different adoption needs.

name: Salt
fit: Dense analytical workspaces, professional tools and interfaces needing adjustable information density.
pros: Density controls, theme tokens and components developed for demanding enterprise workflows.
cons: Specialist grids and charts can involve external integrations; experimental lab components have a different stability level.
note: Inspect core versus lab status. Salt themes for AG Grid or Highcharts do not confer licenses for those products; verify fonts and assets for the chosen theme.

name: SAP UI5 family
fit: Business applications aligned with SAP Fiori, especially alongside an existing SAP landscape.
pros: Enterprise controls, internationalization, themes and compact/cozy density; Web Components can cross framework boundaries.
cons: A family of technologies rather than one interchangeable library; framework and licensing choices affect integration.
note: Choose among OpenUI5, SAPUI5 and UI5 Web Components explicitly. Open-source Web Components are framework-neutral; SAPUI5 distribution and entitlement are separate questions.

name: shadcn/ui
fit: Brand-led products and teams that want direct ownership of component source.
pros: Editable source, composable components, blocks and a registry-based distribution model.
cons: Your team owns consistency, local changes and upstream update reconciliation; copying components is not a maintenance strategy.
note: Treat it as a way to build your component library. Establish ownership, review and upgrade conventions; track which underlying primitives and dependencies each component uses.
